raw_text:
**Cardiac contractility modulation therapy for heart failure**

Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable device therapy designed for patients with symptomatic heart failure (HF) who remain limited despite guideline-directed medical therapy, particularly those with reduced or mildly reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and a narrow QRS complex who are not candidates for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT). The principle emerged from experimental observations that non-excitatory electrical currents delivered during the absolute refractory period can augment myocardial contractility without triggering a new action potential [1,2]. Early canine and isolated-muscle studies established that CCM signals can enhance systolic performance, improve calcium cycling, and influence molecular pathways implicated in HF remodeling [3-6].

Mechanistically, CCM differs fundamentally from pacing or CRT. Contemporary systems deliver high-voltage biphasic impulses to the right ventricular septum after intrinsic activation, during refractoriness, so they do not capture myocardium or alter ventricular activation sequence. Acute effects include increased contractile force and improved calcium handling, whereas chronic exposure appears to induce “reverse molecular remodeling,” including normalization of fetal-gene expression, increased SERCA2a-related signaling, altered phospholamban phosphorylation, and favorable changes in cytoskeletal and extracellular-matrix pathways [7,8]. Importantly, preclinical and translational work suggests that these inotropic effects occur without the myocardial oxygen-consumption penalty associated with conventional pharmacological inotropes [6,7].

The first clinical studies tested CCM in patients with advanced systolic HF and narrow QRS duration. Acute and early feasibility studies showed increases in left ventricular dP/dt and signals of symptomatic improvement [9]. The FIX-HF-4 randomized, double-blind crossover study found improvements in peak oxygen consumption and quality of life, although device-related events and a strong placebo response underscored the complexity of evaluating implantable therapies [10]. The larger FIX-HF-5 trial did not meet all prespecified primary efficacy endpoints in the full cohort, but clinically important benefits were observed in patients with LVEF in the higher reduced range. The subsequent FIX-HF-5C randomized study prospectively enriched this population—NYHA class III or ambulatory IV symptoms, LVEF 25–45%, QRS <130 ms—and demonstrated improvement in peak VO₂, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire score, NYHA class, 6-minute walk distance, and a reduction in the composite of cardiovascular death and HF hospitalization at 24 weeks [11].

Device technology has evolved from systems requiring an atrial sensing lead plus two ventricular leads to a two-lead ventricular-only system. The FIX-HF-5C2 study supported safety and performance of the two-lead Optimizer Smart platform, simplifying implantation and reducing intravascular hardware burden [12]. Observational data suggest that symptomatic and functional benefits may persist for one to two years, with improvements in NYHA class, quality-of-life scores, and LVEF [13,14]. CCM has also been explored in CRT nonresponders, in whom small feasibility studies suggest possible incremental improvement in exercise tolerance and quality of life [15]. Programming questions remain: a small randomized study found no clear advantage of 12 hours versus 5 hours of daily therapy [16], and randomized comparison of one- versus two-ventricular-lead delivery suggested broadly similar short-term clinical effects [17].

Evidence synthesis is broadly consistent: CCM improves patient-centered outcomes more reliably than it improves hard endpoints. Meta-analyses of randomized trials report improvements in quality of life, functional class, peak VO₂, and sometimes 6-minute walk distance, but remain underpowered for mortality [18-20]. Thus, CCM should be viewed as a symptom- and functional-capacity therapy rather than a proven survival therapy. This distinction is central when discussing expectations with patients.

Patient selection is therefore crucial. The best-supported population is patients with persistent NYHA class III symptoms despite optimized HF therapy, LVEF roughly 25–45%, sinus rhythm or sufficient regularity for signal delivery depending on device generation, and QRS duration below conventional CRT thresholds [21]. European and US HF guidelines emphasize foundational pharmacotherapy and established device therapy first; CCM is considered only after optimization of disease-modifying drugs, ICD assessment where appropriate, and exclusion of CRT eligibility [22,23]. Registry and review data suggest that patients with LVEF 35–45% may derive particularly meaningful functional benefit, a range that overlaps heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction [24,25].

The field is expanding. A pilot HFpEF study reported significant improvement in Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire health status after CCM implantation, suggesting that myocardial conditioning may be relevant beyond classic HFrEF [26]. However, HFpEF evidence remains preliminary and requires sham-controlled outcome trials. Contemporary reviews emphasize unresolved questions: durability, interaction with sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors and modern quadruple therapy, optimal lead location, arrhythmia implications, cost-effectiveness, and whether combined CCM-defibrillator systems can reduce total hardware burden [27-30].

In summary, CCM is a biologically plausible and increasingly refined therapy for a treatment gap: symptomatic HF patients with reduced or mildly reduced LVEF and narrow QRS who are not CRT candidates. Its strongest evidence supports improvement in symptoms, quality of life, and exercise capacity. Demonstration of durable reductions in hospitalization and mortality, particularly in the era of modern medical therapy, remains the key requirement for broader adoption.
